options: A user who owns the campaign
A campaign's budget line
A lead or contact attached to a campaign, with a member status such as Sent or Responded
A child campaign in a hierarchy
questions.explain: Campaign Members link leads or contacts to a campaign and carry the status that drives response reporting.

questions.q: Which standard report type gives one row per member so you can see who was reached and how they responded?
options: Campaigns with Campaign Members
Campaigns
Opportunities with Products
Cases
questions.explain: Campaigns with Campaign Members is the reach-and-response report type.

questions.q: Why can the campaign's Num Sent be a risky denominator for response rate?
options: It is calculated from the number of leads
It is often filled in manually or by an integration, so it may be missing or wrong
It is always zero
It can only be seen by administrators
questions.explain: Verify Num Sent exists and is maintained. If not, count members with a 'sent' status and label the denominator clearly.

questions.q: In most orgs, how are opportunities credited to campaigns without Campaign Influence?
options: Every campaign a contact touched shares the credit equally
Credit is split by the amount spent
Credit depends on the campaign's parent only
Through a single Primary Campaign Source field, so one campaign gets the credit
questions.explain: One primary campaign per opportunity means multi-touch influence is invisible without extra features such as Campaign Influence.

questions.q: What is the risk of listing both a parent campaign and its child campaigns in a report using hierarchy statistics?
options: Child campaigns lose their members
Double counting, because the parent's roll-up already includes its children
The report will not run
The parent becomes read-only
questions.explain: Hierarchy statistics roll up the family, so showing parent and children together overstates totals. Choose program level or tactic level.
